slides.heading: 9. Safety, impairment and uncertainty
slides.body: THC can increase anxiety and impair memory or attention. Unwanted effects need to be considered alongside any benefits a person experiences.
slides.replacedBody: Cannabis can worsen anxiety, cognition, motivation, mood or psychosis risk in some people.
slides.passageRef: Author-proposed replacement for the opening sentence. The published page was not changed.
slides.qualification: The first sentence is the acute experimental finding named in Sources. The second sentence is editorial guidance. Motivation, mood and chronic psychosis risk are not claimed from this source.

links.label: D’Souza et al. (2004), Neuropsychopharmacology. DOI 10.1038/sj.npp.1300496. PMID 15173844
links.detail: Randomized, double-blind, counterbalanced acute intravenous THC experiment in 22 healthy cannabis-exposed participants. It measured anxiety, psychosis-like symptoms and cognitive performance. This supports possible acute effects on anxiety, memory or attention. It does not estimate long-term psychotic-disorder incidence, and it does not represent every prescribed flower or oil. It does not substantiate claims about motivation, mood or chronic psychosis risk.

links.label: Second sentence — editorial guidance
links.detail: “Unwanted effects need to be considered alongside any benefits a person experiences.” This is editorial guidance on the proposal card. It is not a finding from D’Souza et al., and the cannabis page was not rewritten.

slides.heading: Driving law is not one UK offence
slides.body: Driving while impaired by a drug is illegal. In England, Scotland and Wales, exceeding a specified drug limit is a separate offence; a statutory medical defence may apply when the medicine was lawfully prescribed or supplied and taken as directed. A prescription does not permit impaired driving. Northern Ireland has a different legal framework.
slides.replacedBody: Driving with THC in the body above legal limits is an offence in the UK, including with a prescription if you are impaired.
slides.passageRef: Proposed replacement for the driving sentence. The article text was not changed. See content/posts/proposed-corrections.json.
slides.qualification: General published-information wording. Not an assessment of any individual driver's legal position.

links.label: GOV.UK: Drug driving law, prescription medicines
links.detail: Official drug-driving law page. A prescription does not permit impaired driving.

links.label: GOV.UK: Drug driving guidance for healthcare professionals
links.detail: Official guidance for healthcare professionals. Not an assessment of any individual driver.

links.label: CPS: Road traffic — drink and drug driving
links.detail: Prosecution guidance. Not the principal healthcare source, and not a substitute for the GOV.UK pages.

slides.heading: What different studies tell us
slides.body: A small controlled trial did not establish an improvement on its main ADHD outcome. A separate UK registry study recorded improvements in anxiety and sleep in people prescribed medical cannabis for ADHD. These findings concern different outcomes and study designs; neither settles how every individual will respond.
slides.replacedBody: Long-term evidence for cannabis in ADHD is limited.
slides.passageRef: Author-proposed replacement for the long-term-evidence sentence. The published page was not changed.
slides.qualification: A non-significant trial result is not proof of no benefit. Registry changes are not a demonstration of core ADHD symptom efficacy. This check is not approval of the cannabis article.

links.label: Cooper et al. (2017). DOI 10.1016/j.euroneuro.2017.05.005. PMID 28576350
links.detail: Six-week randomized placebo-controlled pilot, 30 adults, nabiximols THC:CBD spray. The primary QbTest result was not statistically significant; nominal secondary findings did not survive multiple-testing correction. This is an inconclusive small trial, not proof of no benefit. It does not represent all products or long-term use.

links.label: Ittiphakorn et al. (2023). DOI 10.1002/npr2.12400. PMID 38058251
links.detail: Uncontrolled UK registry series, 68 participants, follow-up to 12 months. Anxiety and sleep scores improved across follow-ups. The general quality-of-life index improved through six months, without a significant baseline difference at 12 months. Eleven participants reported adverse events. There was no comparator, and missing outcomes were imputed. Registry ownership and author clinical or commercial affiliations are disclosed. These limitations qualify the reported changes; they do not erase them. The outcomes were not a direct demonstration of core ADHD symptom efficacy.

links.label: Saunders et al. (2025), expanded evidence panel. DOI 10.1177/10870547251336841
links.detail: Expanded panel, not the two sentences above. Longitudinal chronic-pain cohort, 223 adults across 12 months. No association between medical-cannabis use and ADHD symptom change in the full sample or the moderate/severe subgroup. A limited high-THC association appeared in the minor/no-symptom subgroup. Chronic-pain recruitment limits transfer to a diagnosed ADHD population. This qualifies the registry findings through a different outcome and population. It does not cancel them.

posts.disposition: Hold, off Home and unapproved. Mechanism, short-term symptom ratings and listed unwanted effects are sourced. Emotional regulation and onset remain research questions. Michelson is an abstract-level check, not a full-text extraction.
posts.title: Atomoxetine: a different treatment approach
posts.evidenceNeeded: Emotional regulation and onset remain research questions for the parent article. This narrower citation check does not disprove them. Michelson was not extracted from the full text.

slides.heading: A different mechanism
slides.body: Atomoxetine is a non-stimulant ADHD medicine that blocks the noradrenaline transporter, reducing noradrenaline reuptake.
slides.replacedBody: Broad mechanism: a non-stimulant that mainly increases noradrenaline signalling over time.
slides.passageRef: Author-proposed replacement for the mechanism line. The published page was not changed.
slides.qualification: Product information about the noradrenaline transporter. This wording does not imply dopamine cannot change indirectly.

links.label: Atomoxetine SmPC, section 5.1
links.detail: Professional product information, section 5.1. Not personal advice. Mechanism wording does not imply dopamine cannot change indirectly.

slides.heading: Evidence of benefit
slides.body: Two ten-week placebo-controlled studies in adults found greater improvement in ADHD symptom ratings with atomoxetine. A group result cannot predict an individual's benefit or preferred treatment.
slides.replacedBody: Strengths: may help steadiness, emotional regulation and baseline control; sometimes useful where stimulants are poorly tolerated.
slides.passageRef: Author-proposed replacement for the strengths line. The published page was not changed. The second sentence is editorial guidance.
slides.qualification: A group result is not a prediction for one person. This does not substantiate a universal “less dramatic” experience or the full emotional-regulation claim.

links.label: Michelson et al. (2003). DOI 10.1016/S0006-3223(02)01671-2. PMID 12547466
links.detail: Two randomized double-blind trials, n=280 and n=256, clinician-rated symptoms over ten weeks. Short-term placebo comparison, not a stimulant head-to-head. Abstract-level check, not a full-text extraction. It supports greater symptom improvement than placebo. It does not substantiate a universal subjective “less dramatic” experience or the full emotional-regulation claim.

links.label: Second sentence — editorial guidance
links.detail: “A group result cannot predict an individual's benefit or preferred treatment.” Editorial guidance on this card. Not a sentence from Michelson et al., and the compounds page was not rewritten.

slides.heading: Benefits and tolerability
slides.body: Possible unwanted effects include nausea, reduced appetite, sleep problems, dizziness and fatigue. Blood pressure and heart rate also need monitoring. The aim is useful improvement with tolerable effects.
slides.replacedBody: Limitations: slower onset than stimulants; often less dramatic in day-to-day feel; can cause nausea, fatigue, dizziness or mood effects.
slides.passageRef: Author-proposed replacement for the limitations line. The published page was not changed. The final sentence is editorial guidance.
slides.qualification: The final sentence is editorial guidance. Emotional regulation and onset remain research questions. This check does not disprove them.

links.label: Atomoxetine SmPC, sections 4.4, 4.7 and 4.8
links.detail: Professional product information for warnings, driving and operating machinery, and undesirable effects. Not personal advice. The final sentence of this step is not taken from the SmPC.

links.label: Final sentence — editorial guidance
links.detail: “The aim is useful improvement with tolerable effects.” Editorial guidance on this card. Not a product instruction and not a prediction for one person.

slides.heading: 2009 candidate-gene result, with heterogeneity
slides.body: It found significant associations for several genes, including DAT1, DRD4, DRD5, 5HTT, HTR1B and SNAP25. It also found significant heterogeneity for many of them, meaning the results differed from study to study [1].

Do not quote the 2009 list as if it were the modern GWAS result.

posts.title: VMAT2 and two different proton gradients
posts.previousTitle: Two points that often get muddled
posts.articleTitle: The dopamine supply chain in plain English

visual.alt: Original schematic. A vesicle membrane with V-ATPase pumping H+ from the cytosol into the lumen, and VMAT2 moving monoamine in as H+ moves out. Separate from it, a mitochondrion with outer membrane, intermembrane space, inner membrane and matrix. ATP synthase is on the inner membrane as H+ returns to the matrix. Glycolysis is a second ATP source. No proton arrow joins the organelles.
visual.caption: Original explanatory schematic; not to scale. Vesicle filling and ATP supply involve separate membrane systems.

posts.evidenceNeeded: The public pathway statement that amphetamine inhibits VMAT2 stays open. Ye et al. 2025 is a lead on that question, not a rewrite. The diagram is an original schematic, not a published figure.
posts.openEditorialQuestion: The pathway statement that amphetamine inhibits VMAT2 remains open. Ye et al. 2025, Cell Reports, DOI 10.1016/j.celrep.2025.116490, report amphetamine-induced release of a fluorescent monoamine analogue in VMAT2 proteoliposomes (Figure 4 and S8), consistent with exchange. That does not settle effects at prescribed brain exposures, quantify therapeutic contribution, or establish a patient's response mechanism. The public claim was not rewritten.
posts.learningPoint: Distinguish the proton gradient across a vesicle membrane from the gradient across a mitochondrial membrane.
posts.previousLearningPoint: Gap: a learning point was not supplied. The proposed steps repeat published sentences and do not state a new finding.

slides.heading: The gradient across the vesicle
slides.body: VMAT2 moves dopamine into a vesicle using a proton gradient that the vesicle's own pump (a V-ATPase, which uses ATP) builds across its membrane. It is not driven directly by the mitochondrial proton gradient.
slides.sourceSection: Two points that often get muddled
slides.passageRef: The two gradient sentences, kept on one step. Mechanistic sources are attached here. Earlier related-page links were not the citation marker for this paragraph.
slides.qualification: Tier A on the page is not a source. These two sentences are shown together so the distinction is not delayed. The sources are transporter experiments, not a demonstration of one person's ADHD.

links.label: Ye et al. (2025), Molecular basis of vesicular monoamine transport and neurological drug interactions. DOI 10.1016/j.celrep.2025.116490. PMID 41166311
links.detail: Figure 1B: monoamine uptake and bafilomycin sensitivity. Figure S1C: purified VMAT2 in liposomes, pH-dependent fluorescent-substrate uptake. Direct transporter experiments support proton-gradient dependence. Engineered constructs and model membranes do not establish an individual's disease mechanism. Figure 4 and S8, amphetamine-induced release, stay on the open editorial question and do not rewrite the public pathway claim.

links.label: Neurotransmitter recognition by human vesicular monoamine transporter 2 (2024). DOI 10.1038/s41467-024-51960-z
links.detail: Discussion and Figure 5 support proton-coupled transport. Detailed proposed protonation models should keep their model status.

slides.heading: Where mitochondria fit
slides.body: The vesicle pump uses ATP. Mitochondria help supply ATP, and glycolysis can supply it too. The mitochondrial and vesicle proton gradients are across separate membranes.
slides.replacedBody: Energy supply matters indirectly, through ATP. (Tier A)
slides.sourceSection: Two points that often get muddled
slides.passageRef: Author-proposed replacement for the ATP sentence. The published page was not changed.
slides.qualification: ATP availability is the energy connection. It is not a proton pipe between the organelles, and vesicular ATP need not all come from the adjacent mitochondrion.

links.label: Rangaraju, Calloway and Ryan (2014). DOI 10.1016/j.cell.2013.12.042. PMID 24529383
links.detail: Cultured rat neurons, optical presynaptic ATP measurements and metabolic perturbations, especially Figures 3 and 5. Both glycolysis and mitochondria contributed ATP under the tested conditions. ATP restriction disrupted vesicle cycling and acidification. Not a demonstration of ADHD causation.

links.label: Ye et al. (2025), for the vesicle side of the separation. DOI 10.1016/j.celrep.2025.116490
links.detail: Attached again because the third sentence contrasts the two gradients. VMAT2 uses the vesicular proton gradient. This paper does not show a proton connection from mitochondria, and it does not say all vesicular ATP comes from the adjacent mitochondrion.
